---
title: "A fetal head circumference: the measurement a Dice cannot see"
description: "Ultrasound, an ellipse fitted to a predicted mask, and the one page in this documentation whose answer is a length rather than a score."
mirrors: fetal-head
---

[HC18](https://zenodo.org/records/1327317) is 999 two-dimensional ultrasound images of the
fetal skull, each with an ellipse drawn round it by a sonographer, and a CSV giving every
image's pixel size in millimetres and the head circumference that was recorded. It is CC BY
4.0.

Every other article here ends on an overlap score. This one ends on a **length in
millimetres**, because that is what a clinician writes down and charts against gestational
age. Nobody charts a Dice.

The run below is `examples/measure_fetal_head_circumference.py`, and the weights it produced
are published as `hc18-unet`. Where a number belongs to those published weights rather than
to this run, it says so - the two are different draws of one recipe, and how different is
itself one of the findings.

## Why a circumference is not a score

A Dice asks how many pixels two masks share. A circumference asks how long the boundary of
one of them is. The two fail in different directions, and the directions are the wrong way
round for anybody measuring a length.

**A ragged boundary barely moves an integral over a region.** Add and remove pixels along an
edge in roughly equal measure and the area, and the ellipse fitted to it, hardly move - while
the Dice falls with every one of them.

**A mask that is systematically fat or thin moves it linearly.** Grow the whole outline by a
pixel and the circumference grows with it, every time, in one direction - while the Dice
barely notices, because a one-pixel rim is a small share of a large blob.

So the error a Dice sees best is the one that does not matter here, and the error it sees
worst is the one that does. That is an argument until it is measured, and the last three
sections measure it.

## The data

The archive unpacks to `training_set/` with an image and an `_Annotation.png` beside it, and
`training_set_pixel_size_and_HC.csv` giving the pixel size and the recorded circumference.

The annotation is **a drawn curve rather than a filled region** - an ellipse two or three
pixels wide with nothing inside it - so the region has to be filled before anything can be
trained. The example does that with a hole fill before it builds the configuration, and the
criterion for a usable case falls out of the fill rather than being chosen: a curve that runs
off the edge of the frame encloses nothing, so the fill returns it unchanged.

    186_HC, 346_HC, 628_2HC, 787_HC

Four of the 999, left out. The sonographer's ellipse continues outside the picture, so the
recorded millimetres describe a shape the file does not contain - a limitation of this
instrument rather than a defect in the data, and the reason fitting a conic to the visible
arc is how the literature handles it.

## Splitting by examination, not by image

HC18 names its files `000_HC`, `628_2HC`: the leading number is the **examination**, and
several images can come from one. Dividing at random by file puts an image of an examination
in training and another image of the same examination in the test set, and the score becomes
partly a memory test.

`split.group_by` is where that belongs. It is a regular expression over the sample key, and
the key here is the file name without its extension:

```yaml
split:
  fractions: [0.6, 0.2, 0.2]
  group_by: '^(\d+)_'
  seed: 1
```

995 usable images from 803 examinations. **Three fractions rather than two**, because the
millimetres are reported on the third: no number on this page comes off the data
`early_stopping` watched.

## The specification

```yaml
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: measurements/hc18/cases.csv
  mode: config_file
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
  split:
    fractions: [0.6, 0.2, 0.2]
    group_by: '^(\d+)_'
    seed: 1
models:
  - name: skull
    architecture: u_net
    # 800 x 540 arrives as 800 x 544, which divides by 2^4 and resamples the data almost
    # not at all. A measurement that ends in millimetres should argue with the ellipse,
    # not with the interpolation.
    input_shape: [544, 800]
    blocks: 4
    filters: 16
    batch_size: 4
    epochs: 40
    loss:
      name: cce_dice
    metrics:
      - name: dice
        include_background: false
      - name: iou
        include_background: false
    optimizer:
      name: adam
      learning_rate: 0.001
    callbacks:
      - name: early_stopping
        monitor: val_dice
        patience: 8
        restore_best: true
    augmentation:
      # No vertical flip: an ultrasound fan has a top and a bottom, and a mirrored one is a
      # picture of nothing. The ellipse is symmetric under the horizontal one.
      - name: HorizontalFlip
        params:
          p: 0.5
      - name: RandomBrightnessContrast
        params:
          p: 0.3
```

## Training

```python
from pyplatypus import Engine, from_yaml

engine = Engine(from_yaml("examples/hc18.yaml"))
engine.fit()
```

Forty epochs at 544 x 800, about half an hour on a GTX 1070. The run this page describes
reached a mean Dice of **0.9347** on its held-out third; the published `hc18-unet` weights
are a different draw of the same recipe and reached 0.9494.

Neither number is the point of the page, which is the next three sections.

## From a mask to a millimetre

A prediction is a mask on a grid. A circumference is a length in the world, and what connects
them is the **pixel size**, which is a property of the file rather than of the model.

```python
from pyplatypus import ellipse_circumference

for case, prediction in engine.predict_stream("skull", split="test", space="source"):
    mask = prediction.argmax(axis=-1) == 1
    mm = ellipse_circumference(mask, spacing=(pixel_mm, pixel_mm))
```

Two things in those four lines decide whether the number means anything.

**`space="source"`, not the model's grid.** The pixel size in the CSV describes the image as
it is on disk. A prediction resized to the model's input shape has pixels of a size nobody
recorded, and multiplying by the file's number would be wrong by the ratio of the two shapes.

**`spacing` scales the coordinates, not the answer.** For an area the two are the same thing,
since a count scales by the product of the sides either way. For a *length* they are not: a
perimeter is not separable in its axes, so there is no number to multiply a pixel-space
circumference by unless the pixels happen to be square. Measured on a circle of radius 100 px
at `spacing=(2, 1)`, which is an ellipse of semi-axes 200 and 100: scaling the coordinates
gives 968.9 against 968.8 integrated, where the two scalings somebody reaches for answer
628.3 and 1256.7. HC18's pixels are square, so this example would have been right either way
and would have stopped being right on the first anisotropic dataset.

`ellipse_axes()` returns the two axes if the shape rather than the perimeter is what is
wanted, and `mask_volume()` and `instance_sizes()` are the same idea for areas and volumes.

## What the annotation costs before the model does

Before blaming a model for a millimetre, measure what the pipeline costs with **no model at
all**: put the truth masks through the same ellipse fit and compare with the sonographer's
figures.

    truth masks against the chart, 200 cases      +0.692 mm
    the annotation's drawn line                    2.523 px
    pi * w * pixel predicts                       +0.685 mm
    correlation of prediction with error            0.9994
    left unexplained                               0.008 mm

The floor is **biased rather than noisy** - every case too large by about the same amount -
and the cause is the annotation's own line. The curve a sonographer drew is two and a half
pixels wide, not one; filling it puts the region's boundary half a width outside the curve,
and a radius larger by `w/2` makes a circumference larger by `pi * w`.

That is the difference between an explanation and a guess, and it is why the prediction is
reported **beside** the bias rather than subtracted from it: a correction folded into the
measurement would hide the one number here that is about the dataset rather than about us.

A model reproducing the truth masks perfectly would still read +0.69 mm high. So the model's
own contribution is the comparison against the truth masks rather than against the chart, and
both belong on a page that reports millimetres - the first blames the model for a drawing
convention, the second hides the convention from whoever reads the number.

## The Dice cannot see this error

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/maju116/pyplatypus/main/assets/article-hc18-millimetres.png)

    mean Dice                                       0.9347
    median absolute error                           2.00 mm
    mean absolute error                             5.66 mm
    75th and 90th percentile                  4.43, 12.36 mm
    worst case                                     96.35 mm
    Spearman between the two orderings               0.620

Of the 136 test images scoring 0.95 or better - a figure anybody would publish - **49 are
still wrong by more than 2 mm**, which is 36% of them. On the published weights the same
count is 85 of 144, or 59%.

Read the vertical spread of the right-hand panel at any fixed Dice. A column of points two
orders of magnitude tall is the finding: the score does not tell you what the measurement
will be.

**The median and the mean are both here because they disagree.** The error distribution has a
long tail - half the cases inside 2.00 mm and a tenth outside 12.36 - so the mean describes
the tail rather than a typical case, and the median alone would hide that some images are out
by the width of a head.

## What this does not settle

**One run.** The same recipe trained again gives a different correlation. Four draws of it
have been measured:

    the run on this page                             0.620
    a second                                         0.435
    the published hc18-unet weights                  0.153
    the R vignette's own                             0.458

All four are far from a shared ordering and they span a factor of four. The *direction* is
the finding; the magnitude is one draw, and a single number quoted from this page would
overstate the case at one end.

```python
from pyplatypus import available_weights

available_weights()["hc18-unet"]
```

**A measurement is not a measuring instrument.** The worst case here is out by 96 mm. These
weights are not a biometric tool with a person looking at them, let alone without.

**The ellipse is the shape assumed.** `ellipse_circumference()` fits one, which is right for a
fetal skull and wrong for anything that is not an ellipse - and it measures **one object per
image**, which is HC18's shape rather than the general one. Every object in an image, measured
separately, is `#272` and is not built.

## Notes on the machine

A GTX 1070, which wants the CUDA 12 line of PyTorch; `device_report()` says what the card can
do and `pick_device()` chooses without assuming CUDA. Training is about half an hour at these
settings, and filling the 999 annotations into masks takes a couple of minutes before it.
Nothing on this page depends on which card it was, except how long it took.
